summary: Specifies general rules for how the BIER Algorithm and the IGP Algorithm interact when calculating underlay paths in a Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER) network. It updates RFC 8401 and RFC 8444 and updates the BIER Algorithm registry set up in RFC 8401. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Two sets of instructions both pick routes, and they might disagree. This sets the rules for how they work together so everyone agrees on which road to take.

questions: how do bier and igp algorithms interact
what is the bier algorithm bar
what is the bier igp algorithm ipa field
subtitle: Rules for how a BIER-specific algorithm and a generic IGP algorithm combine to pick multicast forwarding paths.

tldr.problem: BIER routers can name both a BIER-specific algorithm (BAR) and a generic IGP algorithm (IPA) for computing underlay paths, but RFC 8401 and RFC 8444 only allowed value 0 for each and said nothing about how non-zero values interact.
tldr.mechanism: All routers in a sub-domain must use the same BAR and IPA. Each router applies the BIER constraint, then the routing constraint, then runs the BIER algorithm if there is one, and otherwise the IGP algorithm.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 8401 and RFC 8444 and renames the Experimental Use range of the BIER Algorithm registry to Private or Experimental Use.

today: RFC 9272 is a Proposed Standard and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 8401 and RFC 8444.

sections.title: Why BAR and IPA Need Rules
sections.content:
In Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER), a packet carries a BitString, and each bit set stands for an egress router that must receive a copy. Routers forward the packet along underlay paths toward those egress routers. The paths are calculated per sub-domain, using an algorithm specific to that sub-domain. The topology or algorithm may or may not be congruent with unicast, and the algorithm could be BIER-specific or a generic IGP one such as Shortest Path First (SPF).

RFC 8401 and RFC 8444 define an 8-bit BAR (BIER Algorithm) field and an 8-bit IPA (IGP Algorithm) field to signal these choices, but only value 0 is allowed for both. This document sets the general rules for when other values are used.
sections.plainLanguage: A group of friends needs to agree on a route to a party. There are two ways to choose the route, so this document says how to combine them.

sections.title: The IPA and BAR Fields
sections.content:
The definitions in Section 6.1 of RFC 8401 and Section 2.1 of RFC 8444 are replaced. Both fields are one octet.

  • IPA names a generic Routing Algorithm (RA) and its Routing Constraints (RC). Values come from the "IGP Algorithm Types" registry.
  • BAR names a BIER-specific Algorithm (BA) and BIER-specific Constraints (BC) that modify, enhance or replace the calculation defined by the IPA value. Values come from the "BIER Algorithm" registry.

When a BAR value is defined, its BA and BC semantics SHOULD be specified. For an IGP algorithm to be used as a BIER IPA, its RA and RC semantics SHOULD be specified. Anything left unspecified MUST be read as the NULL algorithm or constraint. IGP Algorithm 0 is treated as having a NULL RC, meaning no constraints. A BAR value with no specification MUST come from the Private or Experimental Use range.
sections.plainLanguage: One rule book says how to find the road and the other can add special rules. If a rule book is blank, you act as if it says nothing.

sections.title: General Rules for Combining BAR and IPA
sections.content:
For one sub-domain, all BFRs MUST be provisioned with and signal the same BAR and IPA values. A router that sees another BFR advertise a different BAR or IPA for that sub-domain MUST treat it as incapable of supporting BIER for that sub-domain.

For a topology X associated with a sub-domain, a router calculates underlay paths in four steps:

  1. Apply the BIER constraints to get BC(X). If BC is NULL, BC(X) is X itself.
  2. Apply the routing constraints to get RC(BC(X)). If RC is NULL, this is just BC(X).
  3. Choose the algorithm AG: if BA is NULL, AG is RA; otherwise AG is BA.
  4. Run AG on RC(BC(X)).

The BIER-specific algorithm therefore takes precedence over the IGP one. If the resulting AG is not applicable to BIER, no BIER paths are calculated. The RFC calls this a network design issue that an operator needs to avoid.
sections.plainLanguage: First apply the special BIER rules, then the usual rules, then pick which way of finding the road to use. If the BIER way exists, it wins.

sections.title: When BAR Is Zero, and Worked Examples
sections.content:
BAR value 0 means no BIER-specific algorithm is used, so BA and BC are NULL. The IPA value alone then decides the algorithm and constraints for the sub-domain. Exceptions or extensions to the general rules may be defined later for particular BAR or IPA values, and they must then specify compatibility with defined values.

One example is a new BAR whose BIER-specific constraint is "excluding BIER-incapable routers", with no BIER-specific algorithm. It can go with any IPA, and whatever RC that IPA defines is augmented with the exclusion. If the BC and RC conflict, for example BC excludes BIER-incapable routers and RC includes green links only, and every green link touches a BIER-incapable router, the topology is empty and no forwarding path is found.

A second example is a BAR that specifies the Steiner tree algorithm, used with IPA 0 (which uses SPF). The BIER-specific algorithm takes precedence, so SPF is not used.
sections.plainLanguage: If the extra rules say nothing, the normal way is used alone. If two rules clash so no road is left, you cannot travel, so planners must avoid that.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The "BIER Algorithm" registry is updated in two ways. The "Experimental Use" range is renamed "Private or Experimental Use", and this document is added as a reference for the registry itself and for values 240-254.

On security, the document only sets rules for how BAR and IPA interact. It does not change the security aspects discussed in RFC 8279, RFC 8401 and RFC 8444.
sections.plainLanguage: A label on a shelf in the library was renamed to say it is for private or trial use, and nothing about safety changed.

messages.note: If BC is NULL, BC(X) is X.

messages.label: Apply RC to BC(X)
messages.note: If RC is NULL, RC(BC(X)) is BC(X).

messages.label: Run AG on RC(BC(X))
messages.note: AG is BA if BA is not NULL, otherwise RA.
